ability_damage_tables:
Attack ability damage tables (Bank 01, 121255-121303): one table per player form, three abilities each. Each record is { word $0000, word pointer to the ability's upgrade-level word in WRAM, one damage byte per upgrade level }; the tables hold no animation, sprite-frame or hitbox data.

LoadAbilityDamageA (Will, will_ability_damage_table) and LoadAbilityDamageB (Freedan, freedan_ability_damage_table) in attack_ability_system take the ability index in A, follow the table pointer to the record, read the level from the WRAM word the record points to, and store record[4 + level] in abilityDamageBonus ($09E0 for Will) or rangedDamageBonus ($09E2 for Freedan). combat_collision adds that value to the hit strength.

| Table | Ability | Level word | Damage by level |
|-------|---------|-----------|------------------|
| Will | 0 Psycho Dash | $0B16 | 5 / 10 |
| Will | 1 Psycho Slider | $0B18 | 5 / 8 |
| Will | 2 Spin Dash | $0B1A | 4 / 7 |
| Freedan | 0 Dark Friar | $0B1C | 5 / 8 / 12 |
| Freedan | 1 Aura Barrier | $0B1E | 5 / 9 |
| Freedan | 2 Earthquaker | $0B20 | 0 / 7 |

The level word is written by the jeweler_gem rewards (Psycho Dash level 1 at 20 jewels, Dark Friar level 2 at 30) and, for Dark Friar level 1, by eu97_dark_medicine (it stores $0B1C = 1 when the level is not already 2); the ability code reads it. The other four level words ($0B18, $0B1A, $0B1E, $0B20) have no direct STA in extracted/; not traced: how they get their values. The first word of every record is $0000 and no code reads it. Dark Friar is the only 7-byte record (three levels); the other five are 6 bytes.
body_table:
Player body table (Bank 01, 121201-121254): nine 6-byte body-entry rows that choose the sprite set and the tile graphics the player is drawn with. Row layout: { word spriteset pointer, byte spriteset bank, word tile-graphics source address, byte tile-graphics bank } - the extraction shows it as two long pointers, < @spriteset_X, @gfx >.

Two ways to select a row:
- characterForm x 6: InitActorFromSceneData (scene entry) and actor_pool.SetActorBody copy the spriteset pointer and bank into the actor ($7F0006, $7F0008) and clear playerFlags bit 15. Only rows 0-3 are reached this way.
- SetPlayerSpriteDirect (COP #8E, operand 0-8): writes the same two fields, keeps the table offset in animScratch2 ($7F000E) and the row number in $0AC8, and sets playerFlags bit 15 (sprite override).

DecomposePlayerSprites (sprite_composition) reads row +3 / +5, the tile-graphics source address and bank, for the player's tile DMA list ($06FC / $06FE) in both cases. playerFlags bit 15 only changes where the row offset comes from: animScratch2 when it is set, characterForm x 6 when it is clear. GetPlayerFacingDirection uses $0AC8 - 4 to choose a per-form facing table for rows 4-7.
dialog_dictionaries:
Word dictionaries of the dialogue system (Bank 01, 125864-130340, 4476 bytes): two pointer tables of words, each word a string that ends in the $CA return code and normally includes its trailing space (or punctuation and space), for example 'Attack ', 'Eric: ', 'you. '. A script writes tag $D6 (LU1, DialogCmd_DictionaryA) or $D7 (LU2, DialogCmd_DictionaryB) followed by a 1-byte index; the handler doubles the index, reads the word pointer from the table, and renders the word with a recursive JSL to DialogStringRenderer. DisplaySceneTitle does the same lookup to count characters.

The old note ('~512 compressed word slots', 'Dictionary B: 256 extended words') was wrong on the size: A has 256 words and B has 200 (the index $C7 is the last), 456 words in all (E1, counted in the extracted file). The tables use `&` short pointers and the words follow in address order:

| Part | Table | Words | Total |
|------|-------|-------|-------|
| dialog_dictionary_a | 01EBA8 (512 B) | 01EDA8-01F54C (1957 B) | 2469 B |
| dialog_dictionary_b | 01F54D (400 B) | 01F6DD-01FD23 (1607 B) | 2007 B |

Order (SAMPLED about 6%: the first and last words of each table and the section boundaries): each dictionary is a capitalised section (A $00-$6A, from 'Attack ' to 'Yes, '; B $00-$43, from '1994 ' and 'Actually, ' on) followed by a lowercase section (A $6B-$FF, 'about ' to 'you're '; B $44-$C7, 'always ' to 'you. '), each roughly alphabetical. The words include character names ('Eric: ', 'Erasquez: ', 'Elder ', 'Angel ', 'Ankor '), place and ability names ('Desert ', 'Aura ', 'Attack ') and common words and phrases. 'The most frequently used words (the, you, have)' of the old note was not checked and is dropped.

The extracted dialogue text contains no [LU1] / [LU2] tags (0 hits in extracted/), and db-us/stringTypes.json declares both tables as dictionaries, so the extractor expands the words and rebuild recompresses them; how the compressor decides which words to substitute was not traced (OQ-I070-1). Frequency of use of individual words was not measured.
dialog_template_table:
Dialog template strings (Bank 01, 117397-117669): 22 word pointers ($00-$15) to 22 short dialog strings that the [TPL:nn] control code ($C2, DialogCmd_InsertTemplate) splices into the string being drawn. The handler doubles the operand, switches DBR to this bank, reads the pointer from dialog_template_table and draws the template with a recursive JSL DialogStringRenderer; afterwards it restores the caller's string pointer, the bank and the processor flags, and reloads the cursor from $0998, where the template's last character left it, so a [DLG] template positions the text that follows (the speaker templates only set colours, palette and sound, so they leave the cursor where it was). Most templates select the colours of a speaker.

=== THE TAGS USED HERE (DialogStringRenderer; all numbers in the tags are hex) ===

- [SEP:ii,cccc] (DialogCmd_SetPaletteColor): writes the BGR555 word cccc to CGRAM buffer colour ii ($7F0A00 + ii x 2). The speaker templates write colours $11 and $12, which are entries 1 and 2 of 2bpp palette 4 ($10-$13).
- [PAL:4] (DialogCmd_SetPalette): the following characters use tile palette 4 (palette bits 10-12 of the tile word). Dialog strings return to the normal palette with [PAL:0] at their end.
- [SFX:ss] (DialogCmd_SetSfx): the per-character sound effect id kept in $0996 ([SFX:0] = silent). DialogCmd_OpenDialogueBox resets it to $10, the typing click.
- [DLG:col,row] (DialogCmd_SetPosition) and [SIZ:w,h] (DialogCmd_OpenDialogueBox): put the cursor at a column and row, then open a box w columns wide and h rows high.

=== THE 22 TEMPLATES (uses = occurrences of [TPL:nn] in the extracted strings, comment lines excluded) ===

| Id | Effect | Uses | Seen before |
|----|--------|------|-------------|
| $00 | Will colours, SFX $10 | 222 | Will: and narration (the default) |
| $01 | Kara colours, SFX $1B | 180 | Kara:, Ann:, Vampiress:, Karen: |
| $02 | Lilly colours, SFX $19 | 144 | Lilly:, Vampire:, Girl: |
| $03 | Erik colours, SFX $19 | 82 | Erik:, Lola:, Rofsky:, Queen Edwina:, Ishtar: |
| $04 | Lance colours, SFX $1C | 154 | Lance:, Bill:, Flute:, Elder:, Will's father:, Opponent: |
| $05 | Seth colours, SFX $1A | 27 | Seth:, Sam:, Remus:, Imas: |
| $06 | Neil colours, SFX $1A | 80 | Neil:, Man:, Spectator: |
| $07 | pink / red colours, no SFX | 2 | two lines without a speaker name |
| $08-$0B | box 13 columns x 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 rows at column 3, row 6 (upper box) | 9 / 28 / 303 / 122 | narration and cutscene text |
| $0C-$0F | box 13 columns x 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 rows at column 3, row $11 (the lower default position) | 2 / 4 / 55 / 19 | |
| $10 | the same box as $0F (a duplicate) | 6 | house descriptions |
| $11 | 14 x 3 box at column 2, row $14 and the text 'Where do you go?' | 37 | the route menus ([TPL:11][SFX:0] Quit [N] ...) |

display_preset_table:
PPU display presets (Bank 01, 98304-98867): 47 word pointers ($00-$2E) and the 47 ten-byte records they point to. A scene script picks one with scene command $02 (SceneCmd_ConfigDisplay, scene_script). SceneCmd_ConfigDisplay documents what each byte does; this note adds what the 47 records contain.

Record (in the order they are applied): +0 TM and TMW (main-screen layers), +1 TS and TSW (sub-screen layers), +2 CGWSEL, +3 CGADSUB, +4 layer flags, +5 layerPriorityFlag, +6 BGMODE, +7 scroll/HUD flags, +8 and +9 unused.

| Byte | Values in the 47 records |
|------|--------------------------|
| +0 | $17 x34 (BG1+BG2+BG3+OBJ), $15 x10 (BG1+BG3+OBJ), $11 x2 (BG1+OBJ), $13 x1 (BG1+BG2+OBJ) |
| +1 | $00 x22, $02 x8, $12 x6, $11 x4, $03 x3, $01 x2, $16 x2 |
| +2 | $80 x23, $82 x13, $00 x4, $02 x4, $12 x3 (bit 1 = sub screen is the math addend) |
| +3 | 18 distinct values; bits 0-3 BG1-BG4, bit 4 OBJ, bit 5 backdrop, bit 6 half, bit 7 subtract. Most common: $A1 x6, $41 x5, $A3 x5, $00 x5 |
| +4 | $E4 x13, $A4 x12, $24 x10, $64 x6, $14 x2, $A5, $A6, $65, $66 x1 each: 21 records have bit 6 set (visible height $100), 26 have it clear ($E0); 20 have bit 7 clear |
| +5 | $05 x25, $85 x12, $01 x5, $00 x2, $80, $81, $84 x1 each |
| +6 | $09 x45 (BG mode 1 with BG3 priority), $07 x2 (mode 7: presets $19 and $2D) |
| +7 | $00 x35, $04 x6, $01 x2, $10 x2, $1C x2 (the two mode-7 presets); bit 7 never set, so no preset disables the HUD |
| +8, +9 | $00 in all 47 records |

The pointers run in order: record n is at $01805E + 10 x n, so the table is 94 bytes and the records 470 bytes. Not traced: which scenes use which preset.
enemy_clear_reward_table:
Scene clear reward tier (Bank 01, 109278-109534, 256 bytes), one byte per scene ID ($00-$FF). It is not specific to Dark Space rooms (the old note said 'when all enemies in a Dark Space room are defeated'): any scene whose entry is nonzero pays a permanent stat point once. The tiers are not 'minor/medium/major'; they select the stat:

| Tier | Reward | Scenes |
|------|--------|--------|
| 0 | none | 169 |
| 1 | Max HP + 1 (item $80, pickup e_hp_increase, anim $0C of spriteset_pickups_effects) | 29: $0C $0F $22 $23 $27 $3D $3E $46 $4D $50 $53 $5F $62 $6E $71 $83 $85 $88 $A2 $A4 $A6 $B0 $B3 $B6 $B9 $BC $BE $D2 $D4 |
| 2 | STR + 1 (item $81, e_str_increase, anim $0D) | 27: $0D $1D $20 $26 $3F $45 $4F $52 $60 $65 $6D $6F $84 $87 $A0 $A3 $A8 $B1 $B5 $B7 $BB $CD $D1 $D5 $D7 $D9 $DB |
| 3 | DEF + 1 (item $82, e_def_increase, anim $0E) | 31: $0E $12 $21 $25 $28 $40 $41 $4E $51 $54 $61 $64 $70 $72 $82 $86 $A1 $A5 $A7 $B2 $B4 $B8 $BA $BD $CC $CE $CF $D0 $D3 $D6 $D8 |

Values above 3 do not occur; the readers treat 3 and above as DEF. Whether a scene's reward was already taken is the scene flag $0300 + scene (set when the reward is paid).

Readers: (1) StandardEnemyDefeatHandler.EnemyStatBonusReward: when the last enemy of the scene dies and the flag is clear, spawns the e_hp / e_str / e_def_increase pickup of reward_actors (this also makes the enemy drop a gem only while the reward is already taken or enemies remain, see enemy_stats_table). (2) field_reveal_object: tier & 3 picks the hidden stat item (anim $0C / $0D / $0E, item $80 / $81 / $82). (3) boss_clear_reward_handler.BossClearApplyStatReward: after a boss is defeated, walks a range of scenes and pays every unclaimed tier at once. (4) radar_map_screen: draws the reward frame and icon on the radar while the flag is clear and the tier is nonzero. (The old note's 'draws chest icons' is wrong: chests are drawn from a different list.)
enemy_stats_table:
Enemy combat stat rows (Bank 01, 109552-109991 = $01:ABF0): 110 rows of 4 bytes < HP, ATK, DEF, gemDropType >. The row number is the stats index: byte 6 of an enemy-spawn record in scene_actors (index $01-$63 in 62 distinct values; 0 = an actor without combat stats). InitActorFromSceneData stores index x 4 + the table address in statsPtr ($7F0020,X) and loads byte 0 into currentHp ($7F0026,X). Boss and special actors set statsPtr themselves with an operand such as enemy_stats_table+154 (the offset is in hex: +154 / 4 = row $55).

=== FIELDS (read by combat_collision, StandardEnemyDefeatHandler and field_reveal_object) ===

| Byte | Field | Reader |
|------|-------|--------|
| +0 | HP: the start value of currentHp and the maximum (hitVictimMaxHp) | InitActorFromSceneData, ApplyHitDamageToVictim |
| +1 | ATK: the damage the enemy deals to the player on contact: max(1, ATK - playerDef), then 60 frames of invulnerability | the enemy-hits-player path of combat_collision |
| +2 | DEF: subtracted from the player's total strength: rawDamage = max(1, totalStr - DEF), netDamage = rawDamage + characterForm | ApplyHitDamageToVictim (_DamagePath) |
| +3 | gemDropType: 0 = no gem, 1 = SpawnDropGem1, 2 = SpawnDropGem2, 3 or more = SpawnDropByHpTier (EnemyDropSystem); FieldRevealFromActorStats reads the same byte as value & 3: 0 = nothing, 1 / 2 / 3 = a gem pickup worth 1 / 2 / 5 gems | EnemyGemDropRouter in StandardEnemyDefeatHandler; FieldRevealFromActorStats in field_reveal_object (spawned by EnemyDefeatDispatch for every kill but the last) |

PlayerAttackHitTest (the player's attack box) does not read DEF: its damage is chainDamage / 2 + 1, with chainDamage accumulating over consecutive hits of one attack (formulas in the combat_collision header). Not traced: which attack of the game goes through which of the two routines. DEF $7F (21 rows) and $FF (row $46) therefore do not make an enemy immune: in ApplyHitDamageToVictim they only pin every hit to its minimum, 1 + characterForm. Bit $0010 of the actor's $12 flags is damage / stagger immunity and bit $0020 is the boss bit (EnemyInitBasic sets both): immunity is flag data, not table data.

The gem is only dropped when the scene's clear reward (flag $0300) was already taken or other enemies remain; the last enemy of a scene gives the stat reward of enemy_clear_reward_table instead.

=== WHOLE-TABLE FACTS ===

- 18 rows are all zero ($00 $12 $13 $15-$17 $23-$26 $65-$68 $6A-$6D). Row $00 is also the pointer EnemyInitBasic stores: an actor whose statsPtr equals the table address is counted as 'no stats' (no kill counter, no gem, no reward).
- 92 rows have stats: gemDropType 0 in 37, 1 in 21, 2 in 21, 3 in 13. 21 rows have DEF $7F, row $46 has DEF $FF, rows $21 and $22 have HP $FF.
- Rows named by code (statsPtr operands): $01 dc2F_adrift; $08 ec0E_spiney; $11 ec12_skull_chaser and sp5A_phantom_ribber; $31 and $69 mu67_vampires; $33 gw82_archer; $37 gw8A_sand_fanger; $46 twelve switch, blocker and trapped-slave actors (hit_switch, dm3F_switch, dm40_trapped_slave, ec0E_switch, ec11_aqueduct_blocker, ec11_button_voice, ec12_aqueduct_enemy, ir21_switch, pyD6_vader_barrier_lower / upper, sg52_blocker_enemy_a / b); $47 and $48 awB0_zombie; $4D pyD2_haunt; $55-$58 sE8_dark_gaia (and unused_mode7_boss for $55-$57); $5F and $60 sEA_solid_arm; $64 ec0E_lily and ir29_castoth.
- 16 rows with stats are neither used by a scene spawn record nor named by code: $06 $07 $09 $1F $20 $21 $22 $38 $39 $3B $40 $41 $4B $52 $53 $59.

The enemy a row belongs to is the actor named in the spawn record, so the table does not say which enemy it describes.
event_block_table: Event-triggered tile copy definitions. 158 entries of 8-byte event-block-def structs specifying rectangular tile regions to copy/modify when event flags change. Used for doors, barriers, and puzzle state visual changes.
forced_walk_pan_table:
Camera pan step lists of the forced-walk warps (Bank 01, 108894-109277): 16 word pointers ($00-$0F) to 16 lists that set the speed profile of the camera pan during a forced walk.

=== WHO READS IT ===

An extended warp entry (ExecuteForcedWalkWarp) keeps the list number in the low nibble of its byte 6 (scrollStepTableBase), the direction in bits 4/5/7. The four ForcedWalk* actors in forced_walk look up forced_walk_pan_table[index] and store the pointer in scrollStepTableBase; the CameraPan* handler of the walk direction then calls CameraScrollStepLookup once per pan call.

=== LIST FORMAT ===

A list is a run of little-endian words, ended by a word whose high byte is 0 (always $0000 here). For each word: low byte = delay D, high byte = step S. CameraPan* adds the low nibble of S pixels to the camera target on the call that loads the word and on each of the next D calls, so a word moves the camera S x (D + 1) pixels. The pan ends when the list ends or when the camera target reaches the camera bounds, whichever comes first.

All 16 lists have the same shape: an ease-in of 4 calls each at 1, 2, 4, 6 px (then 8, 10 in the longer ones), a long cruise word, and the mirror ease-out. Only the cruise length changes, which sets the pan distance. The totals are all multiples of 16 pixels (one map block), so every pan covers whole blocks. Each list part note gives its profile and total; the table is 32 bytes, the lists 352 bytes (20 bytes for 12 of them, 28 bytes for the 4 with the longer ramp: $01, $05, $0A, $0F).

| Index | Cruise | Total | Index | Cruise | Total |
|-------|--------|-------|-------|--------|-------|
| $00 | 8 px x 19 | 256 | $08 | 8 px x 29 | 336 |
| $01 | 12 px x 22 | 512 | $09 | 8 px x 31 | 352 |
| $02 | 8 px x 17 | 240 | $0A | 12 px x 42 | 752 |
| $03 | 8 px x 21 | 272 | $0B | 8 px x 35 | 384 |
| $04 | 8 px x 23 | 288 | $0C | 8 px x 47 | 480 |
| $05 | 12 px x 86 | 1280 | $0D | 8 px x 49 | 496 |
| $06 | 8 px x 25 | 304 | $0E | 8 px x 53 | 528 |
| $07 | 8 px x 27 | 320 | $0F | 12 px x 42 | 784 |

Not traced: which warp uses which list.
hdma_ramp_tables: Composite block of HDMA configuration tables and ramp motion curves (121022-121201, Bank 01). Parts: hdma_channel_config (64 bytes, the DMAP transfer mode per B-bus register), hdma_entry_stride_by_mode (13 bytes, of which entries 00-02 are the HDMA entry stride per transfer mode) and the two ramp arc curves behind ramp_motion_curves (64 and 32 frames). The parts are unrelated except for sharing the block; the name hdma_ramp_tables only describes them as a group.
item_pickup_text_table:
Item name strings (Bank 01, 130340-130923): a 64-entry pointer table indexed by item ID ($00-$3F) plus the strings it points to, and five dialogue wrapper strings stored at the end of the block. The 64 strings are the item names (or a short found-message for a few items); the complete messages are the five wrappers.

=== HOW IT IS READ ===

The wrappers contain [ADR:&item_pickup_text_table,DB8]. DialogCmd_IndirectString (DialogStringRenderer) takes the item ID that GiveItemToPlayer stored at $0DB8 (ChestDialogueActor also restores it there) and renders the table entry for that ID in place, so one wrapper prints whichever item was just given. The table is read only through this tag.

| Wrapper | Text | Used by |
|---------|------|---------|
| dialog_item_found | name, 255-frame pause, clear | GiveItem_StoreInSlot (inventory_mgmt): Y returned for a regular pickup |
| dialog_item_full | name, 'Your inventory's full!' | GiveItem_InventoryFull (inventory_mgmt), InteractionDamage_NPCChat in combat_collision (an NPC that gives an item), and chests through GiveItemToPlayer's Y |
| dialog_item_chest | name only | HandleChestInteraction (warps_interaction) overrides Y with it after a successful chest pickup |
| dialog_chest_empty | 'It is empty!' | flag-only chests (warps_interaction); no item name |
| dialog_chest_locked | 'The jewel box is tightly closed.' | chest tile without a scene_chest_table record (warps_interaction); no item name |

The last two are not item strings; they are stored here next to the other chest dialogue. COP #D4 (cop_handlers_inventory) ignores the Y string, so scripts that give items show their own text.

=== ENTRIES ===

The IDs are the inventory item IDs of docs/ram_map.txt ($01 Red Jewel ... $28 Apple).
- Full sentence: $01 'You found a Red Jewel! ', $06 'You found an herb! ', $07 (diamond-shaped block), $0E (Crystal Ball), $13 (Rama's Statue), $14 (Magic Dust), $15-$19 (Teapot), $1A 'It's the Mushroom Drops!'.
- Bare name (the wrapper supplies the rest): $02 'Prison Key ', $03/$04 'Incan Statue A/B ', $05 'Incan Melody ', $08 'Wind Melody ', $09 'Lola's Melody ', $0A 'Large Roast ', $10 'Palace Key'.
- Mystic Statues: $38 'It's a Mystic Statue! ', then seven separate copies of 'Mystic Statue ' for $39-$3F.
- Blank (a single space): $00, $0B, $0C, $0D, $0F, $11, $12 and the 29 IDs $1B-$37, which share one string. These items print nothing through this table.
- $15-$19 all point to the Teapot string, although ram_map names $15-$18 Blue Journal, Lance's Letter, Necklace Stones and Will.

Layout: 128 bytes of pointers + 456 bytes of strings and wrappers.
math_lookup_tables:
Math lookup tables (115588–117397, Bank 01): the default slope speed curves followed by the engine's 8-bit and 16-bit sine/cosine tables. Used by Mode 7 perspective rotation, actor circular/orbital motion, slope physics and the scene-transition wave effect.

=== ADJACENCY CONTRACT ===
Several consumers index past the end of one table and rely on the next table following it in ROM. Do not reorder, resize or relocate these parts independently:

- sine_table_8bit holds only the 64-entry first quarter (0°–90°), yet it is indexed 0–255 (ComputeSineScrollTable, ApplyOrbitalOffsetXY, ApplyOrbitalOffsetFromRef, actor spirals). Entries 64–255 come from signed_cosine_table_8bit, which starts at the 90° peak, so the pair forms a 256-step signed sine (1.406° per step). signed_cosine_table_8bit on its own is the matching 256-step signed cosine.
- sine_table_16bit + cosine_table_16bit + neg_sine_halfwave_16bit form one 512-word sine cycle (0.703° per step): rising quarter, falling quarter, then a negated half-wave. thinkers/mode7_perspective reads it with index ($BC AND $01FF) × 2. Read from cosine_table_16bit the same index gives a 512-word cosine cycle: falling quarter, negated half-wave, then cosine_table_16bit_tail — a copy of the rising quarter that supplies the 270°–360° part (it is not a spare duplicate).

slope_curve_table is not a flag table: its first 64 bytes are the default slope acceleration and deceleration curves (see its part note).
move_chain_table:
Movement delta chains (Bank 01, 110726-115587): 85 word pointers ($00-$54) to chains of delta-nodes, followed by the 1,173 nodes (4,692 bytes, 01B130-01C383). Every movement index in the game is an index into this table: COP movement operands (StageMoveX/Y/XY, StageSpriteMove*, the player Move ops), walk_step_table (forced walks), the world map route steps and the hit stagger all name a chain, not a distance or a speed.

=== NODE AND CHAIN ===

A delta-node is { signed word value, &next }. The value is a per-frame position delta in pixels; the link is the next node. An actor holds the current node pointer in $2C (X chain) or $2E (Y chain): actor_pool.AnimFrameLookup turns an index into the head pointer (table + index x 2), and ApplyMovement / ApplyMovementWithCollision (tile_collision_physics) add the node's value to $14 / $16 once per frame (negated when $12 bit 14 / bit 13 flips the axis) and move the pointer to the link. A zero pointer means no chain: the actor then uses its per-actor scratch delta (moveScratch1/2). The raw index stays in moveXAlt / moveYAlt ($7F0018 / $7F001A).

Each chain ends in exactly one of three ways (counted over the whole file; 85 chains = 1 + 58 + 26):
- null link ($0000): 1 chain, entry $00. The value 0 is applied once and the pointer is cleared.
- link to itself: 58 chains. The last node repeats forever (constant speed, or 0 = stand still after a one-shot curve).
- link back to an earlier node: 26 chains. The chain loops (fractional speeds, oscillations, periodic pulses).

=== FAMILIES (indices) ===

- $00: null chain (value 0, link 0).
- $01-$10: constant +/-1 .. +/-8 pixels per frame, one self-linked node each; odd index = positive, even = negative ($01 = +1, $02 = -1, $03 = +2 ... $0F = +8, $10 = -8).
- $11-$14: fractional constant speeds as 2- and 4-node cycles: $11 +1,0 (+1/2 average), $12 -1,0 (-1/2), $13 +1,0,0,0 (+1/4), $14 -1,0,0,0 (-1/4).
- $15-$54: programmed curves of 1 to 57 nodes: delayed starts (runs of 0), acceleration and deceleration ramps, out-and-back arcs that sum to 0, periodic pulses and pauses (e.g. $3C = +8,0,0,0 repeating, $53 = 16 frames still then 16 frames at -1, repeating). Chain lengths: 1 node ($00-$10, $1F, $20, $37), 2 ($11, $12), 3 ($3F), 4 ($13, $14, $16, $17, $3C), 5 ($51, $52), 6 ($1D, $1E), longest $21 (57), $4C (43), $3D (37), $4D and $4E (33). $16 and $17 are 4-node cycles of +1 / -1 and behave exactly like $01 / $02; $1F, $20 and $37 are a single 0 node that links to itself.
- Node values range from -8 to +12; 0 is the commonest (302 of 1,173 nodes), then +1 (183), -1 (156), +2 (126).

=== USERS ===

- COP movement operands via AnimFrameLookup (cop_handlers_force_move, cop_handlers_sprite, cop_handlers_player_sprite), for example $36 in attack_ability_system and $0F / $10 in ramps.
- forced_walk: walk_step_table byte 1 ($00, $11-$14).
- WorldMapController route steps: three indices per step (X $00CA, Y $00CC, rotation $00BC), see world_map_options.
- hit_stagger_controller: $22 (tier 0, 48 px) and $23 (tier 1 and above, 32 px).
- unused_particle_rain_spawner: indices 3-10.

music_pointer_array: Music ID → SPC data ROM location mapping (bank 01). 30 entries of 3-byte long pointers (addr_lo, addr_hi, bank) to compressed BGM track data. Indexed 1-based: music ID n selects entry n-1 (hdma_dma_spc.asm reads `music_pointer_array-3 + 3n`), so ID $00 never indexes the table. Used by LoadMusicFromTransitionState for ID-driven music loads.
parallax_scroll_table:
Entry index for scanline_band_hdma_thinker (Bank 01, 37 word pointers, $00-$24). The spawn-record parameter byte of the thinker is the index. Each pointer addresses one entry blob: buffer address (word, bank $7E), bank byte, config byte, record size, then records. The format and the decoded contents of every used entry are in the scanline_band_hdma_thinker block note.

The header bytes are NOT a BG mode / layer setting. Config bits 0-5 are the B-bus register index the HDMA channel writes, bit 6 multiplies the camera delta by 16 and bit 7 swaps the scroll sources.

Entries $09, $0C, $0D and $0F-$1A are bare $FFFF words (unused). Types $09 and $19 share one $FFFF word.
scene_chest_table:
Treasure chest placement (Bank 01, 109992-110726 = $01:ADA8): a pointer table of 255 words (scene ID $00-$FE) followed by the chest lists. Only 39 scenes have chests, in 46 records; the other 216 entries point at one shared empty list (chest_list_none, a single $FF byte). The table holds chest records only; a list ends at a record whose first (X) byte has bit 7 set.

=== RECORD (4 bytes, extraction: chest-entry < X, Y, contents, flag >) ===

| Byte | Field |
|------|-------|
| +0 | X tile of the chest's left column. A value with bit 7 set ends the list ($FF in every list) |
| +1 | Y tile of the chest's BOTTOM row (the top row is Y-1) |
| +2 | Contents: the item ID given by GiveItemToPlayer (names in system_strings.item_name_table); 0 = flag-only chest (shows 'It is empty!') |
| +3 | Bits 0-6: event flag ($0200 group, TestEventFlag_0200 / SetEventFlag_0200) set when the chest is opened; bit 7: open with the fanfare (ChestOpeningActor with the music transition) instead of the plain 'found' dialogue |

A chest is 2x2 map tiles: closed $FA/$FB (top row) and $F8/$F9 (bottom row), open $FE/$FF and $FC/$FD. The list is chosen by the scene index $0646 (scene x 2) into the pointer table.

=== READERS ===

- PlaceOpenedChestTiles (warps_interaction): at scene build, every record whose flag is set is drawn open.

scene_warps:
Warp table of all scenes (Bank 01, 98868-108893, 10026 bytes): 255 word pointers, indexed by scene ID ($00-$FE, sceneTableIndex $0646), to 200 `warp-def` lists. InitWarpTable (warps_interaction) reads it when a scene is set up; CheckWarpRectangles tests the player against it every frame. The second list holds forced-walk warps (see below), all of them vertical walks.

=== LIST FORMAT ===

A list is `[scene-warps] $FF [forced-walk warps] $FF`. Both terminators are the single byte $FF (a negative byte 0 ends a list in InitWarpTable, $FF in CheckWarpRectangles); the extractor does not print them, so an empty list is 2 bytes. 200 lists hold 543 scene-warps x 12 B + 200 forced-walk warps x 13 B + 400 B of terminators = 9516 B, and 255 x 2 = 510 B of pointers, which is exactly the 10026 bytes. Pointers share lists: 51 scene IDs point at the empty list warp_def_empty, $E6-$E9 share warp_def_E6 and $EB-$ED share warp_def_EB; 8 lists are empty.

Both kinds start with the trigger rectangle (bytes +0 X tile, +1 Y tile, +2 width, +3 height, in 16-pixel tiles). The player triggers it when playerXTile/YTile fall inside the rectangle AND the pixel position lies in the first (16 x size - 15) pixels (ConvertWarpToPixels).

=== scene-warp (12 bytes): change scene (ExecuteWarp) ===

+4 destination scene (sceneNext $0642), +5 word destination X pixel, +7 word destination Y pixel (warpDestX/Y), +9 facing (warpFacing $0650; the low bits index walk_step_table, bit 7 = save warp: ExecuteWarp also stores the entry in sceneSaveData as the game-over reload point), +10 word packed camera window (warpScrollParams $0652: low byte = offsetY<<4 | offsetX, high byte = boundsY<<4 | boundsX, in 256-pixel units; read by InitCameraBounds). Example: warp_def_01 entry ;00 `< #11, #0D, #02, #02, #08, #$01B8, #$0080, #00, #$1200 >` = trigger tiles ($11,$0D) 2 x 2, go to scene $08 at pixel (440, 128), facing 0, camera window $1200.

Data facts: facing is $00 x225, $03 x229, $06 x32, $07 x32 and $01 x2, plus bit 7 on 23 entries (11 x $80, 9 x $83, 2 x $87, 1 x $86). All 543 entries carry a nonzero camera window (61 distinct values; $1100 x86 and $4400 x84 are the commonest), so the 'normal bounds' path of InitCameraBounds is never taken from this table. 36 entries lead to scene $E6 (sE6_gaia, the Dark Space scene) and all use destination (120, 192), facing 0 and window $1100.

=== forced-walk warp (13 bytes; the extractor type is `stair-warp`) ===

Not a scene change: ExecuteForcedWalkWarp keeps the player in the scene, pans the camera and walks the player by script. Layout by BYTE (the extractor splits it into words at the wrong boundaries): +4/+5 camera window (same packing as above, warpScrollParams), +6 direction and pan list (scrollStepTableBase: bit 7 = north, bits 4/5 = east/west, otherwise south; the low nibble indexes forced_walk_pan_table), +7..+12 a 6-byte walk stream `[direction byte][X offset word][Y offset word][final direction byte]` (the pointer to +7 goes to warpFacing; ForcedWalk* in forced_walk adds the offsets to the player position). Example: warp_def_E3 `stair-warp < #29, #27, #02, #02, #$4430, #$0240, #$0000, #08, #$0301 >` = bytes 29 27 02 02 | 30 44 | 40 | 02 00 00 08 01 03: window $4430, south (bit 6 is not decoded), pan list $00, stream: direction 2, X offset 0, Y offset +$0108 (264 px), final direction 3. The next entry ;01 goes back (byte 6 $80 = north, Y offset $FF10 = -240 px).

Data facts: all 200 are vertical, 100 north (bit 7) and 100 south (bit 6 only, the default). East/West (bits 4/5) never occur, so ForcedWalkEast/West are not reachable from this table. The pan list index in the low nibble of byte 6 is $00 for 143 entries (256-pixel pan), $03 x11, $02 x10, $01 x5, $0D x5, $0E x5 and 21 more spread over $04-$0C and $0F. Not traced: which warp uses which pan list.

=== OTHER NOTES ===

GameOverSequence reloads a warp from the entry+4 pointer stored in reviveWarpPtr ($0AF4; every warp) and sceneSaveData (save warps). The two forced-walk entries of warp_def_03 use unusual first stream bytes ($04, $05); not traced: what the walk does with them.
shared_word_table:
Shared word strings (Bank 01, 125711-125863). 15 console strings that other strings splice in with the text tag [LU:n] (console command $10, ConsoleCmd_InsertSharedWord): the operand byte is the index, and the renderer calls itself on shared_word_table[index]. Each word carries its own trailing space; there is no separator logic.

The words are not only item name prefixes: they also serve ability names ('Psycho Dash', 'Dark Friar'), item descriptions ('Restores strength.', 'Letter from Lance.') and the item menu prompts ('Rearrange items.', 'Select item and enter.'). See the table part note for the index list and which indices are used.

The counts cover the vanilla strings (tables/system_strings, 63 lines carrying 68 tags). The retranslation modules use only the indices $02, $04, $07, $0B and $0C.
system_strings:
The console-string text of the menus (Bank 01, 121304-125711 = $01:D9D8): the boot and title strings, ten pointer tables and the loose strings between them, all drawn by ConsoleStringRenderer. It is read in two ways: RunBg3Script runs a loose string directly (a BG3 script), and the text tag [TBL:@table,addr] picks a table entry with a 16-bit RAM variable as the index (item_name_table by $0AC6, the other tables by $0AE8, character_name_table by $0AD4 and misc_ui_strings by $0B26). Text tags: [N] = line break of one tilemap row, [DBL] = two rows, [LU:n] = shared word n (shared_word_table), [POS:x,y] = cursor, [PAL:n] = palette, [RCC:w,h] = clear (w+1) x (h+1) tiles. The old note called the block 'all game UI text organized into 10 sub-tables'; the dialogue lines are DialogString data elsewhere, and seven of the ten part notes were wrong (see below).

The bytes are $BC $FF $FF $FE $DF $00 $00 $00. Discardable (bit clear): $00, $01 Red Jewel, $06 Herb, $18 Will, $25 Lola's Letter, $28-$3F. Protected: $02-$05, $07-$17, $19-$24, $26 and $27. $18 and $25 being discardable is unexplained (OQ-I072-2).

=== WHAT WAS WRONG IN THE OLD NOTES ===

item_name_line_table was 'longer descriptions shown when hovering': it is the one-line NAME (the description is item_description_table). The blank item range was given as $2A-$38 and the 'Mystic Statue' range as $39-$3F; they are $29-$37 and $38-$3F (8 statues, as the 8 'Mystery Doll' tags of shared_word_table say). item_description_table was 'multi-line descriptions of function and lore': it has 41 entries of short function text. non_discardable_item_bits was 'padding / alignment data between two tables'; it is read by CheckItemDiscardable. misc_ui_strings was 'status labels, save/load prompts, game over text': the table is just 'B' and 'Y' and the loose strings are inventory-menu prompts, tab titles and three screen labels (PAUSE, FORCE, the button legend). The old part notes of item_name_table (blank and statue ranges) and boot_title_strings ('displayed at boot': two of the three are title-screen strings) were also off. character_name_table was 'Will, Kara, Lance, Erik, Seth and other story characters': it holds the three player forms.

Byte check: the ten parts add up to 4407 bytes = 125711 - 121304. Part addresses are from blocks.json; the strings between the tables are listed in the part notes.
walk_step_table:
Walk-step table (Bank 01, 109534-109551): nine 2-byte direction-velocity entries, indexed by a step code $00-$08. Each entry is { byte 0 = player animation index, byte 1 = move_chain_table index (velocity chain) }. The two bytes are read together as one word, animation index in the low byte.

Where the step code comes from and what reads it:
- Scene entry: InitActorFromSceneData indexes the table with the scene's facing value (warpFacing $0650) and stores only byte 0 as the player's initial animation index ($28). The velocity byte is not used there.
- In-scene forced walks (forced_walk): ReadDirSprite_YVelocity / ReadDirSprite_XVelocity fetch one step code per step from the warp's walk-step stream, hand byte 0 to StagePlayerSprFromDP through $0000, and use byte 1 to load the head of a delta-node chain from move_chain_table into $2E (Y axis) or $2C (X axis).

The entries are step codes, not compass directions, and byte 1 is a table index, not a speed (see the part note for the decoded rows).
